persona.who: 49, IT services manager in Pune, 22 years in the same company, laid off last month. Daughter in 11th, home loan, aging mother.
persona.note: twenty two years in one company and they let me go in a 10 minute call. I have not told my mother. Every morning I still wake up at 6 like I have to go to office.

understanding.emotion: ashamed and still tied to the place
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call fear of what might happen, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the verdict you carry alone, and the body still running the old rhythm.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the verdict is theirs to own, and that the harm is letting it replace your own measure.

understanding.core_struggle: An experienced man let go after twenty-two years, carrying the shame and the old routine alone while his parents depend on him.
understanding.mirror: You gave them twenty-two years, and they took it in ten minutes. Now you carry the verdict alone.
understanding.insight: The body knows the old rhythm, but the verdict they handed you is what you are actually carrying, and it is theirs to own, not yours to prove.

queries.hook: Being let go after twenty-two years and carrying the verdict alone, while the body still wakes for a place that no longer has you. I lost my job.
queries.diagnose: When a result goes wrong, the mind turns against itself; the verdict they delivered in ten minutes is not your measure, and the harm deepens only when you begin to believe it.
queries.steady: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they saw; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; learn what this taught you, make amends where you can, and begin again.
queries.story: A man of long service who lost his place and his face, facing the verdict alone and finding the courage to rise again.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: how the world treats someone who has lost money.
verse.sanskrit: तानीन्द्रियाण्यविकलानि तदेव नाम सा बुद्धिरप्रतिहता वचनं तदेव । अर्थोष्मणा विरहितः पुरुषः क्षणेन सोऽप्यन्य एव भवतीति विचित्रमेतत् ॥
verse.line: Same person, same mind, same voice. Lose money, and people suddenly treat you as someone else.
verse.translation: The same faculties, unimpaired; the same name; the same unclouded mind; the same speech. Yet a man deprived of the warmth of wealth becomes, in a moment, someone else. How strange!
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.
verse.misuse: The verse mocks how the world sees you; it does not measure your worth.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to you from the section on wealth. He has watched the world turn its back on the man who has lost his money. He says the same faculties remain, the same mind, the same voice, the same name. Yet a man deprived of the warmth of wealth becomes, in a moment, someone else. How strange.
verse.for_you: You still have the same mind and the same voice after the call. The world around you has changed its tone, but the person who answered that phone twenty-two years ago is still there. The old rhythm belongs to your body, not to your worth.

verse.speaker: Janaka
verse.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
verse.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
verse.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
verse.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
verse.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after hearing wandering sages, questions everything. He decides not to run away from his life. The verse says good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune. You do not have to leave your life to change it. You can do the day's work with a mind that does not clutch.
verse.for_you: You are still on the roof of that old routine, alone with the verdict. The harm is letting that verdict replace your own measure. You can go down and do the day's work, but with a mind that does not clutch.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning, addressed to proud rulers.
verse.sanskrit: हर्तुर्याति न गोचरं किमपि शं पुष्णाति यत् सर्वदा- ऽप्यर्थिभ्यः प्रतिपाद्यमानमनिशं प्राप्नोति वृद्धिं पराम् । कल्पान्तेष्वपि न प्रयाति निधनं विद्याख्यमन्तर्धनं येषां तान् प्रति मानमुज्झत नृपाः कस्तैः सह स्पर्धते ॥
verse.line: Learning is wealth no thief can see. It grows when you give it away and never perishes.
verse.translation: It never comes within a thief's sight; it always nourishes some deep good; given to those who ask, it grows greater; even at the end of an age it does not perish. Kings, drop your pride before those who own this inner wealth called learning. Who can compete with them?
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to proud kings who slight scholars. He says learning is wealth no thief can see. It grows when you give it away and never perishes. Kings, drop your pride before those who own this inner wealth. What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.
verse.for_you: You are keeping the verdict close to you, as if it were the only wealth you own. But the wealth of what you have learned in twenty-two years cannot be taken by a ten-minute call.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a section on steadfastness. He says that praise or blame, money or death, are all passing things. The steady person does not move a step from the right path. The point is that setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.for_you: The old rhythm of the company is gone. The praise and the blame from those twenty-two years are now just noise. Your part is to keep your footing on the path that is right for you now. Let the old routine fall away and hold to what is steady.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
verse.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help'. Arjuna himself asks for help; this is about not abandoning yourself.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult. He says that you could raise yourself by your own self. You do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.for_you: You are the one who must lift yourself. Do not let the verdict of the ten-minute call push you down. Be the friend who holds your own hand today. Choose that friend over the enemy that doubts you.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha on getting through crises.
verse.sanskrit: एकं विवेकं सुहृदमेकां प्रौढसखीं धियम् । आदाय विहरन्नेव संकटेषु न मुह्यति ॥
verse.line: Make good judgment your friend and wisdom your companion, and crises won't bewilder you.
verse.translation: Taking discernment as your one true friend and wisdom as your seasoned companion, you can move through life and not lose your way in crises.
verse.why: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

prasang.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

verse.meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, after two brothers face the death of their parents, the sage Vasishtha tells Rama that a full mind sees a full world. He says that if you take discernment as your true friend and wisdom as your companion, you will not lose your way in a crisis. The point is that grief is love, but endless rumination is a habit you can choose to stop feeding. The old rhythm is in your body now, but the verdict is theirs, and you do not need to prove it to anyone.
verse.for_you: The body remembers the old rhythm of the office, but the verdict belongs to them. Let discernment sit with you today instead of the old story. You are not required to prove anything to anyone.

story.title: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
story.story_hook: For thousands of years the old bird had sat on a mountain with no wings, waiting for a reason.
story.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
story.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

anchor.speaker: Sage Nishakara
anchor.setting: The old vulture Sampati, wings burnt and grounded for ages, is told why he should live on.
anchor.sanskrit: उत्सहेयमहं कर्तुमद्यैव त्वां सपक्षकम्। इहस्थस्त्वं हि लोकानां हितं कार्यं करिष्यसि॥
anchor.line: You are needed exactly where you are, as you are. Your use isn't over.
anchor.translation: I could give you back your wings this very day. But by staying here as you are, you will do something for the good of the world.
anchor.why: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

prasang.title: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
prasang.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
prasang.story_hook: For thousands of years the old bird had sat on a mountain with no wings, waiting for a reason.
prasang.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

story.hook_title: An old bird with burnt wings had waited thousands of years for this moment
story.teaser: An old bird with burnt wings had waited thousands of years for this moment
story.for_you: The old rhythm of the company is gone, but the knowledge you carry from twenty-two years is not. Someone else might need exactly what you know, and your use is not over.

script: You have been carrying the weight of that ten-minute call since it happened. The shame sits in your chest while you manage the house, the parents, and the kids. You are not sure who you are when the work is gone.

Bhartrihari watches the world from a quiet place, noting how it shifts when a man loses his coin. The same eyes, the same mind, the same speech. Yet the moment the wealth vanishes, people look at him as if he were a stranger. And Bhartrihari says: The same faculties, unimpaired. The same name. The same unclouded mind. The same speech. Bhartrihari said:
तानीन्द्रियाण्यविकलानि तदेव नाम सा बुद्धिरप्रतिहता वचनं तदेव, अर्थोष्मणा विरहितः पुरुषः क्षणेन सोऽप्यन्य एव भवतीति विचित्रमेतत्.
In plain words: Same person, same mind, same voice. Lose money, and people suddenly treat you as someone else.

The verse does not say you are less. It says the world changes its tune when the money runs out. Your mind is still sharp. Your voice is still yours. The same name sits on your door. The shame you feel is the echo of how others now sound when they look at you. But that is their shift, not your collapse. The old rhythm returns to the body, not to the soul.
When you walk through the door tonight, notice how your body still knows the old steps. The routine is a ghost, not a verdict. Your worth is not on the line in that ten-minute call.
The world has changed its tone, but you have not.

depth.points: The verse points to the gap between who you are and how the world treats you after money is gone. The faculties remain, but the warmth of wealth is what changes the social air around you. It is the world that shifts, not the core of you.
depth.practice: Notice one moment today when someone treats you differently, and silently name what is still the same in you.
depth.question: What part of you did not change when the call ended?
